Three Seeking Alpha pieces in nine weeks (May 11, June 19) have already published the entire thesis -- the receivables timing, the settlement, the large second-quarter payout. The units respond accordingly: $27.23, about 79% up the 52-week range, roughly 7% above the 200-day average, within about 6% of the 52-week high.

So where do we actually disagree with the market? Not on direction -- on durability. The consensus view is that the coming distribution proves the earnings power. Our reading of the March 8-K says roughly $0.32 per unit of that distribution is Midland County litigation money, and a further slug is a receivables catch-up that was earned in the first quarter. Both are one-time. The disagreement is therefore uncomfortable for the bulls but does not help a buyer: we think the next payout will be even less repeatable than the crowd expects, which is a reason to be more cautious at $27.23, not less. That is a consensus gap that argues for passing, not for entering.

The second disagreement is with our own peer file, which calls this cheap versus peers on a stale anchor to Texas Pacific Land. Against the real comparables it is priced in line. Correcting that removes the last plank of the deep-value case.
forcing_function:
For a deep-value name the question is what event forces the market to re-rate. The honest answer is that the events which could have done so have already happened, and the ones still ahead are routine.

What already fired. The litigation settlement -- $15.5M from the Midland County leasehold dispute -- was finalized March 12 and announced March 16, 2026. That is four months ago. The receivables timing that explained the weak first-quarter payout was disclosed in the 10-Q filed May 6, 2026 and has been public for ten weeks, then amplified by three retail articles. The earnings inflection was reported May 6. Every one of these is spent. The price reflects them: $27.23, near the top of the 52-week range.

What is still ahead, and why none of it re-rates the units. The second-quarter distribution declaration, expected around July 22-23, 2026 based on the partnership's consistent calendar, is genuinely dated and imminent -- roughly a week out. But a quarterly distribution declaration is the ordinary course of business for a vehicle that has declared one every quarter for over twenty years, and this particular number is already widely and correctly anticipated to be large. A telegraphed payout is not a catalyst; it is a scheduled event with the surprise already extracted. If anything the asymmetry is negative -- the payout must clear a high published bar to avoid disappointing.

The Williston acquisition closes July 31, 2026. It is dated and binding, but it is 3,100 net royalty acres for 850,000 units -- about 1.8% dilution against a 48.3-million-unit base. A bolt-on, not a transformation, and the market has priced it as such, correctly. Second-quarter results follow around August 7.

The deeper structural point: this partnership has no re-rating mechanism available to it. The classic forcing functions for a value name -- a buyback authorization, an activist, an asset sale, a dividend initiation, a governance reset, a strategic review -- are all either impossible or meaningless here. There is nothing to activate against: no leverage to fix, no conglomerate to break up, no underearning segment to divest, no governance abuse to correct, no capital being misallocated, and no strategic process a third party could force. Applying the standard activist screens (catalyst density, a sum-of-the-parts discount, activism potential, asymmetric risk and reward) returns a null on all four. The parts do not sum to more than the whole; there is no discount to close.

What this name actually offers is a cash yield from a well-run, debt-free asset. That is a legitimate thing to own. It is not a catalyst, and it should not be underwritten as one.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall -- there is nothing to refinance, because there is essentially no debt (roughly $1M against $28.2M of cash at March 31, 2026), no interest expense, and no capital spending commitment. The partnership cannot get into balance-sheet trouble in any conventional sense. That genuine strength is worth stating plainly before the risks.

The risk here is not solvency. It is disappointment, and it has a probable shape and an approximate date.

The most likely adverse sequence runs as follows. The second-quarter distribution, due to be declared around July 22-23, 2026, is large -- swollen by the roughly $26.9M receivables catch-up and about $15.5M of litigation proceeds. Income-focused buyers, who are the marginal price-setter in this name, see a headline yield and annualize it. Then the third-quarter distribution, declared in late October, normalizes hard, because neither item repeats. The stock de-rates on a payout that was never a run-rate. This is the specific mechanism by which an investor buying today at $27.23 loses money, and it is roughly one to two quarters away.

The macro overlay makes it worse rather than better. Brent sits near $71 and is falling, below where major forecasters expected it to finish the year. This partnership has no operational buffer at all: it cannot hedge in any meaningful way, cannot cut costs it does not have, and cannot raise a price it does not set. Every dollar of oil weakness passes straight through to the cash stream within a quarter. The net profits interests -- about 9% of revenue -- amplify this, because they pay off the operator's profit after costs and so compress far faster than the price decline itself. That is exactly what produced the weak first-quarter payout.

There is also a dated two-sided macro binary sitting inside the window: the US-Iran 60-day ceasefire clock expires around mid-August 2026, and the current market read describes it as more fragile than the headlines suggest. Re-escalation would spike oil and this name with it; a durable peace would push oil lower still. Neither outcome is knowable, and neither is an edge -- it is uncompensated exposure to a coin-flip that happens to sit right on top of the position.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling pressure to exploit here, and that absence is a core reason this is a pass rather than a watchlist item.

The shareholder base is exactly what the structure selects for: income-focused retail owners and yield funds who hold for the variable quarterly payout. Nothing is about to force them out mechanically. There is no dividend cut on the horizon -- quite the opposite, the next payout is set to be unusually large. There is no strategic pivot to alienate them, no index deletion, no lock-up expiry, no leverage covenant that could force a liquidation. The partnership has paid a distribution every quarter for over two decades, through the 2008, 2015-16 and 2020 oil collapses. This holder base is not going to be shaken out; it is about to be rewarded, briefly.

That is the problem. The washout we would want to buy into is not coming -- it has already been skipped. The units sit near a 52-week high with the good news published and a big distribution about to land. If anything the flow pressure over the next few weeks runs the wrong way: a large declared payout tends to attract yield-chasing buyers into an already-extended price, which is the opposite of the setup we underwrite.

The genuine mechanical dynamic worth naming runs against existing owners rather than for them. Dorchester funds acquisitions by issuing units -- 850,000 of them for the Williston acreage closing July 31, 2026, on top of a base that has grown from about 39.6 million units in early 2024 to 48.3 million now, roughly 22% in two years. Each issuance is a small, permanent transfer of the per-unit cash stream. It is not forced selling, but it is a persistent structural headwind to per-unit value that a yield-focused base tends not to track.

The one flow signal pointing the right way is insider behaviour: 64 open-market purchases totalling 205,759 units against zero sales. That is real alignment and it is why this is a pass rather than a short. But steady insider accumulation across a range of prices signals belief in the asset, not a view that today's price is low.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now -- and to be clear about why, because the reason is unusual: this is a genuinely fine business that we simply cannot buy at this price.

Everything admirable about Dorchester Minerals is true. It owns perpetual mineral and royalty interests across 28 states -- a property right about as durable as an asset gets, since nobody can produce the hydrocarbons beneath that acreage without paying Dorchester first. It carries net cash of about $27M with essentially no debt and no interest expense, at a time when leverage defines its sector. It spends nothing on capital, so free cash flow equals operating cash flow at a margin near 87%. It earns about 28.9% on invested capital. Its earnings just grew about 67% year over year. Insiders have bought in the open market 64 times and sold zero. It has paid a distribution every quarter for over two decades, through three oil collapses, and it has quietly compounded book value per unit at about 12.7% annually by buying acreage with its own units through a tax structure competitors cannot replicate. Management promises nothing and delivers a mechanical payout. That earns a credibility score of 4 and my genuine respect.

None of that is the question. The question is price, and three findings settle it.

First, the deep-value signal that surfaced this name is an artifact. The -66% margin of safety comes from a model that is structurally wrong for a depleting royalty partnership -- the same model set that simultaneously prints a $9.19 fair value and a $67.60 discounted-cash-flow value on the same day. A seven-fold disagreement is a broken model, not a hidden edge, and neither number carries weight.

Second, the peer discount does not exist. Our peer file's cheap-versus-peers verdict anchors to Texas Pacific Land, which is not a comparable -- it is a surface-land and water-infrastructure corporation in the S&P 500 trading at about 40.6x EBITDA for reasons that have nothing to do with royalty economics. Against the real structural twins, Black Stone Minerals and Kimbell Royalty Partners, Dorchester trades at about 9.24x versus their 9.32x and 9.82x. In line. My parts-based work lands in the same place from a different direction -- about $25.50 per unit against a live price of $27.23 -- and when two independent methods agree that a stock is roughly 7% above fair value, I believe them.

Third, and this is the finding that turns a neutral into a pass: the good news is not merely priced, it is partly borrowed from the future. The second-quarter distribution due around July 22-23 will be large, and roughly $0.32 per unit of it is Midland County litigation money received in April, with a further slug being first-quarter receivables arriving late. Both are one-time. The published bull case is right that the payout will be big and wrong to treat it as evidence of run-rate earnings power. The most probable path from here is a large July payout, yield-chasers buying an already-extended price, and a hard normalization in the October declaration.

On timing and the current market backdrop, every consideration points the same way. The regime prizes independence from any single shared macro factor and explicitly warns against theses hinging on oil -- and this is a 100% pure-play bet on oil with zero operational buffer, no hedging, and no pricing power whatsoever. Oil is deflating, with Brent near $71 and falling below where forecasters expected it to end the year, which flows straight through to this cash stream within a quarter. The fat lane right now is structural special situations -- spin-offs and forced sellers -- and this is neither. A fragile ceasefire clock expiring around mid-August sits inside the holding window as an uncompensated coin-flip. And the load-bearing catalysts are spent: the settlement announced four months ago, the timing disclosure ten weeks ago. What remains ahead -- a telegraphed quarterly distribution and a 1.8%-dilution bolt-on closing July 31 -- is the ordinary course of business, not a re-rating event. There is no forced-selling pressure to buy into, no activist lever to pull, and nothing to break up.

On the moat I am deliberately departing from the mechanical rule, and the director should see the reasoning. Returns have roughly halved from their 45.9% peak to about 28.9%, which the house rule would read as an eroding moat capping the value score at 3. I call it narrow but stable instead, because the decline is traceable almost entirely to oil falling from about $100 in 2022 to about $70 now -- a price cycle, not a franchise decay. The decisive counter-evidence is that earnings rebounded about 67% the moment prices recovered; eroding moats do not do that, because their damage is one-way. The acreage base is growing, not melting, and book value per unit keeps compounding. It is narrow rather than wide for a different and more fundamental reason: a business with literally no pricing power -- a pure price-taker on a global commodity -- does not have a wide moat however good its returns look at the top of a cycle. On the energy transition, the threat is manageable rather than terminal on any horizon we underwrite: oil demand is at record highs, and Permian and Bakken barrels are the lowest-cost in America, which makes them the last cut in a shrinking-demand world, not the first.

So the cap never binds, and it does not need to. Value conviction is 2 on the arithmetic alone: a high-quality asset trading about 7% above a fair-value estimate that two independent methods agree on offers no margin of safety, and quality does not substitute for price. Execution conviction is also 2, for the separate reason that the catalyst is spent and the macro tilt is actively hostile. The two scores land in the same place here by coincidence, not by default -- the value case fails on price, the catalyst case fails on timing.

This is a name to admire and revisit, not to own today. The specific level that would make it interesting: the high teens to low twenties -- at or below the adverse case near $17, or meaningfully under the $25.50 fair value -- which a genuine oil flush toward $60 Brent could deliver, most plausibly after the October distribution normalizes and the yield-chasers who bought the July headline discover what they actually bought. Buy the disappointment, not the announcement.

interrogator_dossier:
# Dorchester Minerals, L.P. (DMLP) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-07-16. Price used throughout: $27.23 per common unit (NASDAQ, live quote 2026-07-16). All figures in US dollars.*

**A note on sources, stated up front.** Dorchester Minerals does not hold earnings calls. There is no transcript for this name — not in our paid data feed, and not anywhere else, because none exists. The partnership has never hosted one. It communicates with owners through short press releases (typically 200–400 words), quarterly filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and nothing more. There is no investor day, no guidance, no management presentation deck.

That absence is itself the most important forensic fact about this company, and this dossier treats it as evidence rather than as a gap. Everything below is built from filings, dated press releases, live market data, and the screener's financial trajectory. Where a normal dossier would test management's words against their numbers, here there are almost no words to test. I have not invented any.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The takeaway: there is no narrative arc, and that is deliberate.**

Most companies tell a story that evolves — a growth driver introduced here, quietly dropped there. Dorchester tells no story at all. The partnership owns oil and gas mineral and royalty interests across 28 states and collects a share of whatever the operators drilling on that land produce and sell. It has no employees drilling anything, no capital spending, and no operational plan to narrate. Management's public communication over the last several years has been mechanically consistent: announce the quarterly cash distribution, announce the quarterly result, occasionally announce an acquisition. That is the whole arc.

What *has* changed is the scale of the asset base, and here the record is genuinely active:

- **Unit count has grown from roughly 39.6 million (Q1 2024) to 48.3 million (Q1 2026)** — about 22% growth in two years. This is not dilution for its own sake. Dorchester's signature model is the non-taxable contribution-and-exchange: landowners hand over mineral acreage and receive newly issued units instead of cash, deferring their tax bill. The partnership buys assets without spending cash or borrowing.
- **The most recent instance is dated and live.** On July 3, 2026 (announced July 6), Dorchester agreed to acquire roughly 3,100 net royalty acres across five counties in the Williston Basin, North Dakota, in exchange for 850,000 common units, with closing expected July 31, 2026. Cash received by the contributing entities on or after April 1, 2026 comes to the partnership at closing.

So the honest arc is: *a static, deliberately boring cash-collection machine that has been quietly and steadily enlarging its acreage footprint using its own units as currency.* No thesis was introduced and no thesis was dropped, because none was ever offered.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Management makes almost no claims. The one recurring statement in the quarterly releases is a caution *against* over-reading the numbers — that "cash distributions are not comparable to its net earnings due to timing and other differences including depletion" (Q1 2026 release, May 6, 2026). This is a company warning investors not to expect too much, which is the opposite of the usual forensic problem.

The interesting test is therefore not management-versus-numbers but **screener-narrative-versus-numbers**, because the scan data feeding this committee is materially stale and, read carelessly, points the wrong way.

| Claim / input | The actual evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Revenue declining: −5.4% year over year, three-year annual decline of 3.6%" | True for fiscal 2025, but **already reversed**. Q1 2026 revenue was $58.9M against $43.2M a year earlier — up about 36%. Trailing-twelve-month revenue is ~$168M versus the $153M fiscal-2025 figure. | **Stale — the trend has already turned** |
| "Earnings collapsing: EPS $1.20, down 43.7% year over year" | The fiscal-2025 figure is real but backward-looking. Q1 2026 delivered $0.59–0.60 per unit against $0.36 a year earlier — up about 67%. Trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS is $1.44, not $1.20. | **Stale — understates current earnings power by ~20%** |
| "Margin sits 2.04 standard deviations below its historical peak" | Accurate, and worth understanding rather than fearing. The peak was fiscal 2022, when oil averaged near $100. Net income fell from $131M (2022) to $57M (2025) as prices normalized. This is a **price** effect, not a business-quality effect. | **True but misread** |
| "Return on invested capital 45.9%" | The live trailing-twelve-month figure is **28.9%**, not 45.9%. Returns are exceptional but have roughly halved from the 2022 commodity peak. | **Overstated — the honest number is lower and falling** |
| "Net debt −$41M" (scan) / "net cash $27M" (live correction) | The live correction is right: cash of $28.2M against ~$1M of total debt at March 31, 2026. Current ratio 16.6x. This is a genuinely unlevered balance sheet. | **Live correction verified** |
| "Insider buy ratio 5.00" (scan) / "64 open-market buys, 205,759 units, zero sells" (live correction) | The live correction is the signal that matters. Zero open-market sales against 64 purchases is an unusually clean insider record. | **Live correction verified — a real signal** |
| "Fair value $9.19, margin of safety −66%" (Buffett model); "DCF fair value $67.6" | These two models disagree by a factor of **seven**. Per-method results range from +60% (discounted cash flow) to −100% (IV15). | **Both are unusable — see below** |

**The most important forensic point in this dossier:** when a valuation model says $9.19 and another says $67.60 on the same company on the same day, the models have not found an edge — they have broken. Both are mis-specified for a depleting royalty partnership. The Buffett/Graham style models penalize a business for having a shrinking earnings base and no reinvestment, which is not a defect here but the *design*: Dorchester deliberately returns nearly all cash rather than reinvesting it. The discounted-cash-flow model does the opposite error, capitalizing an 86.7% free-cash-flow margin into perpetuity as though the underlying wells will not deplete. Neither the −66% margin of safety nor the +60% one should be given any weight. The valuation must be built from the cash stream directly, which the Architect section does.

**Where the narrative is poorer than the trajectory justifies:** the screener paints a shrinking, deteriorating business. The live quarter shows a company whose earnings just grew 67% year over year with a stronger balance sheet than it has had in years. The scan is looking at a 2025 oil-price trough and calling it a decline.

**Where the narrative is richer than the trajectory justifies:** the two widely-read Seeking Alpha pieces (May 11 and June 19, 2026) arguing the coming payout will exceed $1.10 per unit are directionally right but rest partly on a one-time item, which section 7 unpacks. That is the real hazard here — not management's storytelling, but the *market's*.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable — and structurally untestable.**

There is no tone to trace. Dorchester issues no guidance, holds no calls, and takes no analyst questions. The quarterly releases have not meaningfully changed in wording or length in years. There is no shift from offensive to defensive language, because there is no language.

The one genuine confidence signal is not verbal but financial, and it is strong: **64 open-market insider purchases totalling 205,759 units against zero sales.** People who work at a partnership this small — the general partner is a handful of people in Dallas — buying units in the open market, repeatedly, with no offsetting sales, is a more reliable confidence indicator than any quantity of management commentary. It cannot be rehearsed and it costs them real money.

Set against that: the buying is not necessarily *timing* information. Insiders at a royalty partnership buy for yield and for alignment, often mechanically. A steady drumbeat of purchases at a range of prices tells you they believe in the asset; it does not tell you the units are cheap today.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High — by construction, not by achievement.**

Dorchester has never issued guidance, so it has never missed guidance. There is no sandbagging pattern to detect because there is no forecast to sandbag. This scores as high reliability, but the director should read that score correctly: **it reflects the absence of the opportunity to lie, not a demonstrated record of hitting hard targets.** A company that promises nothing cannot disappoint on promises. It can still disappoint on cash.

What the partnership *does* commit to is mechanical and it has honoured it without interruption: it distributes essentially all cash actually received in a quarter, less minimal expenses. That commitment has been kept for over two decades, through the 2008, 2015–16 and 2020 oil collapses. The payout varies enormously — that is the deal — but it has always been made.

One credibility nuance worth flagging, because it looks like a miss and is not. The Q1 2026 distribution of **$0.475036 per unit (declared April 23, 2026, paid May 14)** looks alarmingly weak against reported earnings of $0.59 per unit for the same quarter. It was not an operational failure. Operating cash flow in Q1 2026 was only $23.9M against $50.0M of EBITDA because **receivables built by $26.9M in the quarter** — cash Dorchester had earned but had not yet been paid. Because the payout is based on cash *received*, not revenue *booked*, the money simply slipped into the following quarter. Management flagged exactly this in the release ("timing and other differences"), and the 10-Q filed May 6, 2026 documents it. They told the truth in advance, in one sentence, and were largely ignored for a month until analysts read the filing.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

There are no analyst questions to review — no calls, and no meaningful sell-side coverage of this listing. Our own data provider carries no analyst price-target coverage for DMLP, and I could not source a current consensus target from any dated public source. **I am therefore not using any price target in this analysis, rather than assuming one.**

The relevant pressure is coming from a different direction: **retail commentary is running well ahead of the filings.** Three Seeking Alpha articles in nine weeks (May 11, June 19 twice) have promoted the same idea — that the weak Q1 payout was a timing artifact and the Q2 payout will be dramatically larger. They are right on the mechanics. The concern is that this is now a *crowded, published* insight rather than a private one, on a stock trading 79% of the way up its 52-week range.

The question nobody is asking, and the one that matters: **how much of the coming payout is repeatable?**

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 **Green flags**

- **Q1 2026 earnings up ~67% year over year** ($0.59–0.60 vs $0.36 per unit) on revenue up ~36% — the strongest year-over-year growth in several years, driven by higher realized prices, higher production, and recent Rockies/Permian additions.
- **A genuinely clean balance sheet**: $28.2M cash against ~$1M debt at March 31, 2026 — net cash of ~$27M, current ratio 16.6x, no interest expense at all. In a sector defined by leverage, this is rare and real.
- **64 open-market insider buys, zero sells.**
- **Book value per unit compounding ~12.7% annually over five years**, even as EPS fell ~11.3% annually over the same span — the tell that the acquisition machine is genuinely adding asset value while commodity prices dragged on earnings.
- **The unit-for-acreage model works and is still running** — the Williston deal announced July 6, 2026 is the latest proof.
- **Zero capital expenditure, structurally.** Free cash flow equals operating cash flow, quarter after quarter. Operators bear all drilling cost; Dorchester takes a share off the top.

🔴 **Red flags**

- **Returns are high but falling: return on invested capital ~28.9% today against the 45.9% the scan reports from the peak.** Roughly halved.
- **Zero pricing power.** This is the central structural fact. Dorchester cannot raise a price, cut a cost, or win a customer. Its revenue is a fixed percentage of a global commodity price set entirely elsewhere. It is a pure price-taker.
- **The asset depletes.** Every barrel produced permanently reduces the remaining resource. Absent continuous acquisitions, the cash stream shrinks. The partnership must keep issuing units to stand still — the 22% unit growth in two years is the cost of that treadmill.
- **The load-bearing good news is already public and already old.** The $15.5M litigation settlement (Midland County, Texas) was finalized March 12 and announced March 16, 2026 — four months ago. The receivables timing was disclosed May 6. Neither is news.
- **Net profits interests are the fragile part.** Unlike royalties, which pay off gross revenue, net profits interests pay off the operator's *profit* after costs — so in a weak price year they compress far faster than royalties, and can reach zero. This segment is ~9% of revenue and carries disproportionate downside.
- **The stock is not washed out.** At $27.23 it sits 79% up its 52-week range, ~7% above its 200-day average, and within 6% of its 52-week high of $28.95. Whatever this setup is, it is not distress.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The one-time item hiding inside the "big Q2 payout" thesis.** This is the most valuable finding in this dossier and it requires reading the March 8-K rather than the June commentary.

The $15.5M settlement of the Midland County leasehold litigation was, per the dated filing, received by the Operating Partnership and **included in the calculation of the April 2026 net profits interest payment**. April sits in the second quarter. So the Q2 2026 distribution — expected to be declared around July 22–23, 2026 based on the partnership's consistent calendar — will contain roughly **$15.5M ÷ 48.3M units ≈ $0.32 per unit of pure one-time litigation proceeds**, alongside the ~$26.9M receivables catch-up from Q1.

This means the coming payout will be large, and it will be *correctly* large, and it will also be **substantially non-repeatable**. An investor who annualizes it will overpay badly. The bull commentary calling for ">$1.10 per unit" is arithmetically reasonable; the error is in what an investor does with that number afterwards. A single quarter carrying a timing catch-up *plus* a litigation windfall is not a run-rate — it is two non-recurring items stacked in one distribution.

**A terminology signal in the acquisition release.** The July 6 announcement describes a "non-taxable contribution and exchange agreement with unrelated third parties." That phrasing is doing real work: the sellers are taking units rather than cash specifically to defer tax. It tells you Dorchester's true competitive advantage is not operational skill but **tax structure** — it can offer a landowner something a cash buyer cannot. That is a durable and underrated edge, and it explains why the partnership can keep acquiring without ever touching the debt market.

**What the size of the deal quietly says.** 3,100 net royalty acres for 850,000 units is about 1.8% dilution against a 48.3-million-unit base. This is a bolt-on, not a transformation. The market has priced it as such — correctly. Anyone treating the July 31 closing as a re-rating event is mistaking a routine transaction for a catalyst.

**Capital allocation has not drifted.** Dividends paid have run in a tight $33–36M band for five consecutive quarters while cash held steady near $28–42M. There is no empire-building, no buyback theatre, no debt-funded adventure. The discipline is genuine and consistent.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

This is a well-run, honestly-run, structurally clean partnership doing exactly what it says it does, with insiders buying alongside outside owners and a balance sheet carrying no debt at all. Management deserves credit. The business deserves respect.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *the quality of this business and the attractiveness of this price are two entirely different questions, and only the first one is favourable.* Every genuinely good fact here — the 67% earnings rebound, the net cash, the insider buying, the coming large distribution — is already public, already dated, and already in a $27.23 price sitting near a 52-week high. The one piece of non-obvious work in this dossier (the $0.32 per unit of litigation money inside the coming payout) makes the setup *less* attractive, not more, because it means the headline yield about to be printed overstates the repeatable one. The director is not being offered a mispricing. He is being offered a fair price for a fine asset, at a moment when the crowd has just figured out that the next dividend is big.

**Economic moat: NARROW. Moat trend: STABLE.**

The moat type is a **property right** — a perpetual mineral interest, which is about as legally durable as an asset gets. Nobody can produce the hydrocarbons under Dorchester's acreage without paying Dorchester first. It cannot be competed away, innovated around, or disrupted by a better product. Layered on top is a **tax-structure advantage** (the non-taxable exchange) that lets the partnership buy acreage rivals must pay cash for.

But it is narrow, not wide, and the evidence forces that call. A wide moat implies pricing power, and Dorchester has literally none — its revenue is a fixed share of a price set by OPEC, shale operators and global demand. Returns on invested capital have roughly halved from the peak to 28.9%, gross margin is contracting, and the earnings base fell 57% from 2022 to 2025. A business that cannot influence its own selling price does not have a wide moat, however excellent its returns look at the top of a cycle.

**Why I am calling the trend STABLE rather than ERODING, explicitly and against the mechanical rule.** The house rule says a high-but-falling return on capital indicates an eroding moat. Applied blindly here it would give the wrong answer, and the director should see the reasoning. The decline from 45.9% to 28.9% is traceable, almost entirely, to oil falling from roughly $100 in 2022 to roughly $70 now. It is a *price* cycle, not a franchise decay. The decisive piece of counter-evidence: **Q1 2026 earnings grew 67% year over year the moment prices recovered.** A structurally eroding franchise does not rebound 67% in a quarter on a modest price move — an eroding moat's damage is one-way and permanent. Meanwhile the acreage base is *growing* (Williston, plus recent Rockies and Permian additions) and book value per unit is compounding at ~12.7% annually. The asset is not melting; the commodity is oscillating.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The relevant structural force is fossil-fuel demand displacement through electrification. It is real, and over a multi-decade horizon it caps the terminal value of carbon-linked assets. But on any horizon this committee can underwrite, it does not impair Dorchester: global oil demand is at record highs, and Dorchester's acreage sits in the Permian, Bakken and Anadarko — the lowest-cost barrels in the United States. In a shrinking-demand world, the low-cost barrel is the *last* one cut, not the first. This is not linear-media decline, where the product itself is being abandoned. Applicable theme: **energy-transition-loser**, held at manageable rather than material or terminal.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither — and this is the finding the director most needs. **It is not cheap at all.** The screener's −66% margin of safety comes from a model that is structurally wrong for a depleting royalty. Measured against the only honest live comparison — the two genuine structural twins, Black Stone Minerals and Kimbell Royalty Partners, both royalty partnerships with variable payouts — Dorchester trades at ~9.2x enterprise value to EBITDA against their ~9.3x and ~9.8x. It is priced **exactly in line**. There is no discount to explain, no fear to exploit, and no trap to avoid. There is a good business at a fair price.

---

bull_thesis:
The bull case rests on a simple, verifiable claim: this is an exceptional business whose reported numbers understate what it earns today. Dorchester Minerals owns oil and gas mineral and royalty interests across 28 states. It collects a share of what operators produce on its land, spends nothing on drilling, and hands nearly all the cash to owners each quarter. The screener that surfaced this name is reading a stale year. It reports revenue down about 5% and earnings per unit of $1.20, down about 44% -- both true of fiscal 2025, and both already reversed. In the first quarter of 2026 revenue was $58.9M against $43.2M a year earlier (up about 36%) and earnings were $0.59 per unit against $0.36 (up about 67%). Trailing-twelve-month earnings are $1.44 per unit, not $1.20. The fiscal-2025 trough was an oil-price trough, not a business failure.

The balance sheet is genuinely rare for this sector: $28.2M of cash against roughly $1M of total debt at March 31, 2026 -- net cash of about $27M, a current ratio of 16.6x, and no interest expense whatsoever. Because operators bear every dollar of drilling cost, there is no capital spending at all; free cash flow simply equals operating cash flow, quarter after quarter, at a free-cash-flow margin near 87%. Return on invested capital is about 28.9% on the trailing twelve months.

Insiders are voting with money: 64 open-market purchases totalling 205,759 units against zero sales. At a partnership this small -- the general partner is a handful of people in Dallas -- that is a costly, unfakeable signal, and far more informative than the grant-inflated ratio in the raw scan.

The acquisition machine still works. Dorchester's signature move is the non-taxable contribution and exchange: landowners hand over acreage and take newly issued units instead of cash, deferring their tax bill. That is a structural advantage a cash buyer cannot match, and it lets the partnership grow without ever borrowing. It has compounded book value per unit at about 12.7% annually over five years even while earnings per unit fell about 11.3% annually on lower prices -- the tell that real asset value was being added underneath the commodity noise. The latest instance is dated and live: on July 3, 2026 (announced July 6) Dorchester agreed to acquire roughly 3,100 net royalty acres across five North Dakota counties in the Williston Basin for 850,000 common units, expected to close July 31, 2026.

The near-term cash story is also real. The disappointing first-quarter distribution of $0.475036 per unit (declared April 23, paid May 14) was a timing artifact, not a shortfall: operating cash flow was only $23.9M against $50.0M of EBITDA because receivables built by $26.9M -- money earned but not yet collected. Because the payout is based on cash actually received, that cash simply moves into the second quarter. Layered on top, the $15.5M Midland County litigation settlement (finalized March 12, announced March 16, 2026) was included in the April 2026 net profits interest payment, which also falls in the second quarter. The distribution due to be declared around July 22-23, 2026 should therefore be materially larger than the last one.

For the bull case to work, three conditions must hold: oil must stabilize at or above roughly $70-75 Brent; Permian and Bakken operators must keep drilling Dorchester's acreage at current pace; and the unit-funded acquisition programme must keep replacing depletion at accretive terms. If all three hold, an owner collects a high-single-digit to low-double-digit cash yield from a debt-free, capital-light asset with a permanent property right at its core.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not dispute that this is a good business. It disputes the price, and it identifies what the enthusiastic commentary is quietly double-counting.

First and most important: the coming distribution is inflated by items that will not repeat. The second-quarter payout will contain roughly $15.5M of litigation proceeds -- about $0.32 per unit on 48.3M units -- plus the roughly $26.9M receivables catch-up that slipped out of the first quarter. Both are one-time. An investor who sees the headline number and annualizes it will badly overpay. The two widely-read Seeking Alpha pieces (May 11 and June 19, 2026) arguing the payout will exceed $1.10 per unit are arithmetically defensible; the danger is what a reader does with that figure next. A single quarter stacking a timing catch-up on top of a legal windfall is not a run-rate.

Second, none of the good news is private. The settlement was announced March 16 -- four months ago. The receivables timing was disclosed in the 10-Q filed May 6 and has been public for ten weeks. Three retail articles in nine weeks have broadcast the whole thesis. Meanwhile the units trade at $27.23, roughly 79% of the way up the 52-week range, about 7% above the 200-day average, and within about 6% of the 52-week high of $28.95. This is not a neglected, washed-out asset. It is a well-covered idea whose good news has already been paid for.

Third, the structural weaknesses are real. Dorchester has zero pricing power -- it cannot raise a price, cut a cost, or win a customer, because its revenue is a fixed share of a global commodity price set entirely elsewhere. It is a pure price-taker. The asset depletes: every barrel produced permanently reduces what remains, so the partnership must keep issuing units simply to stand still. Unit count has grown from about 39.6 million in the first quarter of 2024 to 48.3 million in the first quarter of 2026 -- roughly 22% in two years. That is the cost of the treadmill, and it is a real cost to existing owners. Returns have roughly halved from their peak, to about 28.9%.

Fourth, the net profits interests -- about 9% of revenue -- are structurally fragile. Unlike royalties, which pay off gross revenue, these pay off the operator's profit after costs. In a weak price year they compress far faster than royalties and can go to zero. This is precisely the mechanism that made the first quarter look so poor.

Fifth, the macro setup is a headwind, not a tailwind. Brent is around $71 and falling, below where major forecasters expected it to end the year. Every dollar of oil weakness flows directly and immediately into this cash stream with no operational buffer whatsoever. The single-factor exposure is total.

What would confirm the bear case: oil settling into the $60-65 range, which would compress both royalty cash and, far more violently, the net profits interests; a visible slowdown in operator drilling on Dorchester's acreage; or -- the most likely near-term confirmation -- a large second-quarter distribution followed by a sharp normalization in the third, exposing the one-time items and disappointing buyers who annualized the peak.

On timing and the current market backdrop, every consideration points the same way. What remains ahead -- a telegraphed quarterly distribution and a 1.8%-dilution bolt-on closing July 31 -- is the ordinary course of business, not a re-rating event. On the moat I am deliberately departing from the mechanical rule, and the director should see the reasoning. Returns have roughly halved from their 45.9% peak to about 28.9%, which the house rule would read as an eroding moat capping the value score at 3. I call it narrow but stable instead, because the decline is traceable almost entirely to oil falling from about $100 in 2022 to about $70 now -- a price cycle, not a franchise decay. The decisive counter-evidence is that earnings rebounded about 67% the moment prices recovered; eroding moats do not do that, because their damage is one-way. On the energy transition, the threat is manageable rather than terminal on any horizon we underwrite: oil demand is at record highs, and Permian and Bakken barrels are the lowest-cost in America, which makes them the last cut in a shrinking-demand world, not the first.

So the cap never binds, and it does not need to. Value conviction is 2 on the arithmetic alone: a high-quality asset trading about 7% above a fair-value estimate that two independent methods agree on offers no margin of safety, and quality does not substitute for price. Execution conviction is also 2, for the separate reason that the catalyst is spent and the macro tilt is actively hostile. The two scores land in the same place here by coincidence, not by default -- the value case fails on price, the catalyst case fails on timing.

This is a name to admire and revisit, not to own today. # Dorchester Minerals, L.P. (DMLP) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-07-16. Price used throughout: $27.23 per common unit (NASDAQ, live quote 2026-07-16). All figures in US dollars.*

**A note on sources, stated up front.** Dorchester Minerals does not hold earnings calls. There is no transcript for this name — not in our paid data feed, and not anywhere else, because none exists. The partnership has never hosted one. It communicates with owners through short press releases (typically 200–400 words), quarterly filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and nothing more. There is no investor day, no guidance, no management presentation deck.

That absence is itself the most important forensic fact about this company, and this dossier treats it as evidence rather than as a gap. Everything below is built from filings, dated press releases, live market data, and the screener's financial trajectory. Where a normal dossier would test management's words against their numbers, here there are almost no words to test. I have not invented any.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The takeaway: there is no narrative arc, and that is deliberate.**

Most companies tell a story that evolves — a growth driver introduced here, quietly dropped there. Dorchester tells no story at all. The partnership owns oil and gas mineral and royalty interests across 28 states and collects a share of whatever the operators drilling on that land produce and sell. It has no employees drilling anything, no capital spending, and no operational plan to narrate. Management's public communication over the last several years has been mechanically consistent: announce the quarterly cash distribution, announce the quarterly result, occasionally announce an acquisition. That is the whole arc.

What *has* changed is the scale of the asset base, and here the record is genuinely active:

- **Unit count has grown from roughly 39.6 million (Q1 2024) to 48.3 million (Q1 2026)** — about 22% growth in two years. This is not dilution for its own sake. Dorchester's signature model is the non-taxable contribution-and-exchange: landowners hand over mineral acreage and receive newly issued units instead of cash, deferring their tax bill. The partnership buys assets without spending cash or borrowing.
- **The most recent instance is dated and live.** On July 3, 2026 (announced July 6), Dorchester agreed to acquire roughly 3,100 net royalty acres across five counties in the Williston Basin, North Dakota, in exchange for 850,000 common units, with closing expected July 31, 2026. Cash received by the contributing entities on or after April 1, 2026 comes to the partnership at closing.

So the honest arc is: *a static, deliberately boring cash-collection machine that has been quietly and steadily enlarging its acreage footprint using its own units as currency.* No thesis was introduced and no thesis was dropped, because none was ever offered.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Management makes almost no claims. The one recurring statement in the quarterly releases is a caution *against* over-reading the numbers — that "cash distributions are not comparable to its net earnings due to timing and other differences including depletion" (Q1 2026 release, May 6, 2026). This is a company warning investors not to expect too much, which is the opposite of the usual forensic problem.

The interesting test is therefore not management-versus-numbers but **screener-narrative-versus-numbers**, because the scan data feeding this committee is materially stale and, read carelessly, points the wrong way.

| Claim / input | The actual evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Revenue declining: −5.4% year over year, three-year annual decline of 3.6%" | True for fiscal 2025, but **already reversed**. Q1 2026 revenue was $58.9M against $43.2M a year earlier — up about 36%. Trailing-twelve-month revenue is ~$168M versus the $153M fiscal-2025 figure. | **Stale — the trend has already turned** |
| "Earnings collapsing: EPS $1.20, down 43.7% year over year" | The fiscal-2025 figure is real but backward-looking. Q1 2026 delivered $0.59–0.60 per unit against $0.36 a year earlier — up about 67%. Trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS is $1.44, not $1.20. | **Stale — understates current earnings power by ~20%** |
| "Margin sits 2.04 standard deviations below its historical peak" | Accurate, and worth understanding rather than fearing. The peak was fiscal 2022, when oil averaged near $100. Net income fell from $131M (2022) to $57M (2025) as prices normalized. This is a **price** effect, not a business-quality effect. | **True but misread** |
| "Return on invested capital 45.9%" | The live trailing-twelve-month figure is **28.9%**, not 45.9%. Returns are exceptional but have roughly halved from the 2022 commodity peak. | **Overstated — the honest number is lower and falling** |
| "Net debt −$41M" (scan) / "net cash $27M" (live correction) | The live correction is right: cash of $28.2M against ~$1M of total debt at March 31, 2026. Current ratio 16.6x. This is a genuinely unlevered balance sheet. | **Live correction verified** |
| "Insider buy ratio 5.00" (scan) / "64 open-market buys, 205,759 units, zero sells" (live correction) | The live correction is the signal that matters. Zero open-market sales against 64 purchases is an unusually clean insider record. | **Live correction verified — a real signal** |
| "Fair value $9.19, margin of safety −66%" (Buffett model); "DCF fair value $67.6" | These two models disagree by a factor of **seven**. Per-method results range from +60% (discounted cash flow) to −100% (IV15). | **Both are unusable — see below** |

**The most important forensic point in this dossier:** when a valuation model says $9.19 and another says $67.60 on the same company on the same day, the models have not found an edge — they have broken. Both are mis-specified for a depleting royalty partnership. The Buffett/Graham style models penalize a business for having a shrinking earnings base and no reinvestment, which is not a defect here but the *design*: Dorchester deliberately returns nearly all cash rather than reinvesting it. The discounted-cash-flow model does the opposite error, capitalizing an 86.7% free-cash-flow margin into perpetuity as though the underlying wells will not deplete. Neither the −66% margin of safety nor the +60% one should be given any weight. The valuation must be built from the cash stream directly, which the Architect section does.

**Where the narrative is poorer than the trajectory justifies:** the screener paints a shrinking, deteriorating business. The live quarter shows a company whose earnings just grew 67% year over year with a stronger balance sheet than it has had in years. The scan is looking at a 2025 oil-price trough and calling it a decline.

**Where the narrative is richer than the trajectory justifies:** the two widely-read Seeking Alpha pieces (May 11 and June 19, 2026) arguing the coming payout will exceed $1.10 per unit are directionally right but rest partly on a one-time item, which section 7 unpacks. That is the real hazard here — not management's storytelling, but the *market's*.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable — and structurally untestable.**

There is no tone to trace. Dorchester issues no guidance, holds no calls, and takes no analyst questions. The quarterly releases have not meaningfully changed in wording or length in years. There is no shift from offensive to defensive language, because there is no language.

The one genuine confidence signal is not verbal but financial, and it is strong: **64 open-market insider purchases totalling 205,759 units against zero sales.** People who work at a partnership this small — the general partner is a handful of people in Dallas — buying units in the open market, repeatedly, with no offsetting sales, is a more reliable confidence indicator than any quantity of management commentary. It cannot be rehearsed and it costs them real money.

Set against that: the buying is not necessarily *timing* information. Insiders at a royalty partnership buy for yield and for alignment, often mechanically. A steady drumbeat of purchases at a range of prices tells you they believe in the asset; it does not tell you the units are cheap today.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High — by construction, not by achievement.**

Dorchester has never issued guidance, so it has never missed guidance. There is no sandbagging pattern to detect because there is no forecast to sandbag. This scores as high reliability, but the director should read that score correctly: **it reflects the absence of the opportunity to lie, not a demonstrated record of hitting hard targets.** A company that promises nothing cannot disappoint on promises. It can still disappoint on cash.

What the partnership *does* commit to is mechanical and it has honoured it without interruption: it distributes essentially all cash actually received in a quarter, less minimal expenses. That commitment has been kept for over two decades, through the 2008, 2015–16 and 2020 oil collapses. The payout varies enormously — that is the deal — but it has always been made.

One credibility nuance worth flagging, because it looks like a miss and is not. The Q1 2026 distribution of **$0.475036 per unit (declared April 23, 2026, paid May 14)** looks alarmingly weak against reported earnings of $0.59 per unit for the same quarter. It was not an operational failure. Operating cash flow in Q1 2026 was only $23.9M against $50.0M of EBITDA because **receivables built by $26.9M in the quarter** — cash Dorchester had earned but had not yet been paid. Because the payout is based on cash *received*, not revenue *booked*, the money simply slipped into the following quarter. Management flagged exactly this in the release ("timing and other differences"), and the 10-Q filed May 6, 2026 documents it. They told the truth in advance, in one sentence, and were largely ignored for a month until analysts read the filing.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

There are no analyst questions to review — no calls, and no meaningful sell-side coverage of this listing. Our own data provider carries no analyst price-target coverage for DMLP, and I could not source a current consensus target from any dated public source. **I am therefore not using any price target in this analysis, rather than assuming one.**

The relevant pressure is coming from a different direction: **retail commentary is running well ahead of the filings.** Three Seeking Alpha articles in nine weeks (May 11, June 19 twice) have promoted the same idea — that the weak Q1 payout was a timing artifact and the Q2 payout will be dramatically larger. They are right on the mechanics. The concern is that this is now a *crowded, published* insight rather than a private one, on a stock trading 79% of the way up its 52-week range.

The question nobody is asking, and the one that matters: **how much of the coming payout is repeatable?**

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 **Green flags**

- **Q1 2026 earnings up ~67% year over year** ($0.59–0.60 vs $0.36 per unit) on revenue up ~36% — the strongest year-over-year growth in several years, driven by higher realized prices, higher production, and recent Rockies/Permian additions.
- **A genuinely clean balance sheet**: $28.2M cash against ~$1M debt at March 31, 2026 — net cash of ~$27M, current ratio 16.6x, no interest expense at all. In a sector defined by leverage, this is rare and real.
- **64 open-market insider buys, zero sells.**
- **Book value per unit compounding ~12.7% annually over five years**, even as EPS fell ~11.3% annually over the same span — the tell that the acquisition machine is genuinely adding asset value while commodity prices dragged on earnings.
- **The unit-for-acreage model works and is still running** — the Williston deal announced July 6, 2026 is the latest proof.
- **Zero capital expenditure, structurally.** Free cash flow equals operating cash flow, quarter after quarter. Operators bear all drilling cost; Dorchester takes a share off the top.

🔴 **Red flags**

- **Returns are high but falling: return on invested capital ~28.9% today against the 45.9% the scan reports from the peak.** Roughly halved.
- **Zero pricing power.** This is the central structural fact. Dorchester cannot raise a price, cut a cost, or win a customer. Its revenue is a fixed percentage of a global commodity price set entirely elsewhere. It is a pure price-taker.
- **The asset depletes.** Every barrel produced permanently reduces the remaining resource. Absent continuous acquisitions, the cash stream shrinks. The partnership must keep issuing units to stand still — the 22% unit growth in two years is the cost of that treadmill.
- **The load-bearing good news is already public and already old.** The $15.5M litigation settlement (Midland County, Texas) was finalized March 12 and announced March 16, 2026 — four months ago. The receivables timing was disclosed May 6. Neither is news.
- **Net profits interests are the fragile part.** Unlike royalties, which pay off gross revenue, net profits interests pay off the operator's *profit* after costs — so in a weak price year they compress far faster than royalties, and can reach zero. This segment is ~9% of revenue and carries disproportionate downside.
- **The stock is not washed out.** At $27.23 it sits 79% up its 52-week range, ~7% above its 200-day average, and within 6% of its 52-week high of $28.95. Whatever this setup is, it is not distress.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The one-time item hiding inside the "big Q2 payout" thesis.** This is the most valuable finding in this dossier and it requires reading the March 8-K rather than the June commentary.

The $15.5M settlement of the Midland County leasehold litigation was, per the dated filing, received by the Operating Partnership and **included in the calculation of the April 2026 net profits interest payment**. April sits in the second quarter. So the Q2 2026 distribution — expected to be declared around July 22–23, 2026 based on the partnership's consistent calendar — will contain roughly **$15.5M ÷ 48.3M units ≈ $0.32 per unit of pure one-time litigation proceeds**, alongside the ~$26.9M receivables catch-up from Q1.

This means the coming payout will be large, and it will be *correctly* large, and it will also be **substantially non-repeatable**. An investor who annualizes it will overpay badly. The bull commentary calling for ">$1.10 per unit" is arithmetically reasonable; the error is in what an investor does with that number afterwards. A single quarter carrying a timing catch-up *plus* a litigation windfall is not a run-rate — it is two non-recurring items stacked in one distribution.

**A terminology signal in the acquisition release.** The July 6 announcement describes a "non-taxable contribution and exchange agreement with unrelated third parties." That phrasing is doing real work: the sellers are taking units rather than cash specifically to defer tax. It tells you Dorchester's true competitive advantage is not operational skill but **tax structure** — it can offer a landowner something a cash buyer cannot. That is a durable and underrated edge, and it explains why the partnership can keep acquiring without ever touching the debt market.

**What the size of the deal quietly says.** 3,100 net royalty acres for 850,000 units is about 1.8% dilution against a 48.3-million-unit base. This is a bolt-on, not a transformation. The market has priced it as such — correctly. Anyone treating the July 31 closing as a re-rating event is mistaking a routine transaction for a catalyst.

**Capital allocation has not drifted.** Dividends paid have run in a tight $33–36M band for five consecutive quarters while cash held steady near $28–42M. There is no empire-building, no buyback theatre, no debt-funded adventure. The discipline is genuine and consistent.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

This is a well-run, honestly-run, structurally clean partnership doing exactly what it says it does, with insiders buying alongside outside owners and a balance sheet carrying no debt at all. Management deserves credit. The business deserves respect.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *the quality of this business and the attractiveness of this price are two entirely different questions, and only the first one is favourable.* Every genuinely good fact here — the 67% earnings rebound, the net cash, the insider buying, the coming large distribution — is already public, already dated, and already in a $27.23 price sitting near a 52-week high. The one piece of non-obvious work in this dossier (the $0.32 per unit of litigation money inside the coming payout) makes the setup *less* attractive, not more, because it means the headline yield about to be printed overstates the repeatable one. The director is not being offered a mispricing. He is being offered a fair price for a fine asset, at a moment when the crowd has just figured out that the next dividend is big.

**Economic moat: NARROW. Moat trend: STABLE.**

The moat type is a **property right** — a perpetual mineral interest, which is about as legally durable as an asset gets. Nobody can produce the hydrocarbons under Dorchester's acreage without paying Dorchester first. It cannot be competed away, innovated around, or disrupted by a better product. Layered on top is a **tax-structure advantage** (the non-taxable exchange) that lets the partnership buy acreage rivals must pay cash for.

But it is narrow, not wide, and the evidence forces that call. A wide moat implies pricing power, and Dorchester has literally none — its revenue is a fixed share of a price set by OPEC, shale operators and global demand. Returns on invested capital have roughly halved from the peak to 28.9%, gross margin is contracting, and the earnings base fell 57% from 2022 to 2025. A business that cannot influence its own selling price does not have a wide moat, however excellent its returns look at the top of a cycle.

**Why I am calling the trend STABLE rather than ERODING, explicitly and against the mechanical rule.** The house rule says a high-but-falling return on capital indicates an eroding moat. Applied blindly here it would give the wrong answer, and the director should see the reasoning. The decline from 45.9% to 28.9% is traceable, almost entirely, to oil falling from roughly $100 in 2022 to roughly $70 now. It is a *price* cycle, not a franchise decay. The decisive piece of counter-evidence: **Q1 2026 earnings grew 67% year over year the moment prices recovered.** A structurally eroding franchise does not rebound 67% in a quarter on a modest price move — an eroding moat's damage is one-way and permanent. Meanwhile the acreage base is *growing* (Williston, plus recent Rockies and Permian additions) and book value per unit is compounding at ~12.7% annually. The asset is not melting; the commodity is oscillating.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The relevant structural force is fossil-fuel demand displacement through electrification. It is real, and over a multi-decade horizon it caps the terminal value of carbon-linked assets. But on any horizon this committee can underwrite, it does not impair Dorchester: global oil demand is at record highs, and Dorchester's acreage sits in the Permian, Bakken and Anadarko — the lowest-cost barrels in the United States. In a shrinking-demand world, the low-cost barrel is the *last* one cut, not the first. This is not linear-media decline, where the product itself is being abandoned. Applicable theme: **energy-transition-loser**, held at manageable rather than material or terminal.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither — and this is the finding the director most needs. **It is not cheap at all.** The screener's −66% margin of safety comes from a model that is structurally wrong for a depleting royalty. Measured against the only honest live comparison — the two genuine structural twins, Black Stone Minerals and Kimbell Royalty Partners, both royalty partnerships with variable payouts — Dorchester trades at ~9.2x enterprise value to EBITDA against their ~9.3x and ~9.8x. It is priced **exactly in line**. There is no discount to explain, no fear to exploit, and no trap to avoid. There is a good business at a fair price.

---

The net profits interests -- about 9% of revenue -- amplify this, because they pay off the operator's profit after costs and so compress far faster than the price decline itself. That is exactly what produced the weak first-quarter payout.

There is also a dated two-sided macro binary sitting inside the window: the US-Iran 60-day ceasefire clock expires around mid-August 2026, and the current market read describes it as more fragile than the headlines suggest. Re-escalation would spike oil and this name with it; a durable peace would push oil lower still. Neither outcome is knowable, and neither is an edge -- it is uncompensated exposure to a coin-flip that happens to sit right on top of the position.

If anything the flow pressure over the next few weeks runs the wrong way: a large declared payout tends to attract yield-chasing buyers into an already-extended price, which is the opposite of the setup we underwrite.

Each issuance is a small, permanent transfer of the per-unit cash stream. It is not forced selling, but it is a persistent structural headwind to per-unit value that a yield-focused base tends not to track.

The one flow signal pointing the right way is insider behaviour: 64 open-market purchases totalling 205,759 units against zero sales. moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now -- and to be clear about why, because the reason is unusual: this is a genuinely fine business that we simply cannot buy at this price.

Everything admirable about Dorchester Minerals is true. It owns perpetual mineral and royalty interests across 28 states -- a property right about as durable as an asset gets, since nobody can produce the hydrocarbons beneath that acreage without paying Dorchester first. It carries net cash of about $27M with essentially no debt and no interest expense, at a time when leverage defines its sector. It spends nothing on capital, so free cash flow equals operating cash flow at a margin near 87%. It earns about 28.9% on invested capital. Its earnings just grew about 67% year over year. Insiders have bought in the open market 64 times and sold zero. It has paid a distribution every quarter for over two decades, through three oil collapses, and it has quietly compounded book value per unit at about 12.7% annually by buying acreage with its own units through a tax structure competitors cannot replicate. Management promises nothing and delivers a mechanical payout. That earns a credibility score of 4 and my genuine respect.

None of that is the question. The question is price, and three findings settle it.

First, the deep-value signal that surfaced this name is an artifact. The -66% margin of safety comes from a model that is structurally wrong for a depleting royalty partnership -- the same model set that simultaneously prints a $9.19 fair value and a $67.60 discounted-cash-flow value on the same day. A seven-fold disagreement is a broken model, not a hidden edge, and neither number carries weight.

Second, the peer discount does not exist. Our peer file's cheap-versus-peers verdict anchors to Texas Pacific Land, which is not a comparable -- it is a surface-land and water-infrastructure corporation in the S&P 500 trading at about 40.6x EBITDA for reasons that have nothing to do with royalty economics. Against the real structural twins, Black Stone Minerals and Kimbell Royalty Partners, Dorchester trades at about 9.24x versus their 9.32x and 9.82x. In line. My parts-based work lands in the same place from a different direction -- about $25.50 per unit against a live price of $27.23 -- and when two independent methods agree that a stock is roughly 7% above fair value, I believe them.

Third, and this is the finding that turns a neutral into a pass: the good news is not merely priced, it is partly borrowed from the future. The second-quarter distribution due around July 22-23 will be large, and roughly $0.32 per unit of it is Midland County litigation money received in April, with a further slug being first-quarter receivables arriving late. Both are one-time. The published bull case is right that the payout will be big and wrong to treat it as evidence of run-rate earnings power. The most probable path from here is a large July payout, yield-chasers buying an already-extended price, and a hard normalization in the October declaration.

On timing and the current market backdrop, every consideration points the same way. The regime prizes independence from any single shared macro factor and explicitly warns against theses hinging on oil -- and this is a 100% pure-play bet on oil with zero operational buffer, no hedging, and no pricing power whatsoever. Oil is deflating, with Brent near $71 and falling below where forecasters expected it to end the year, which flows straight through to this cash stream within a quarter. The fat lane right now is structural special situations -- spin-offs and forced sellers -- and this is neither. A fragile ceasefire clock expiring around mid-August sits inside the holding window as an uncompensated coin-flip. And the load-bearing catalysts are spent: the settlement announced four months ago, the timing disclosure ten weeks ago. What remains ahead -- a telegraphed quarterly distribution and a 1.8%-dilution bolt-on closing July 31 -- is the ordinary course of business, not a re-rating event. There is no forced-selling pressure to buy into, no activist lever to pull, and nothing to break up.

On the moat I am deliberately departing from the mechanical rule, and the director should see the reasoning. Returns have roughly halved from their 45.9% peak to about 28.9%, which the house rule would read as an eroding moat capping the value score at 3. I call it narrow but stable instead, because the decline is traceable almost entirely to oil falling from about $100 in 2022 to about $70 now -- a price cycle, not a franchise decay. The decisive counter-evidence is that earnings rebounded about 67% the moment prices recovered; eroding moats do not do that, because their damage is one-way. The acreage base is growing, not melting, and book value per unit keeps compounding. It is narrow rather than wide for a different and more fundamental reason: a business with literally no pricing power -- a pure price-taker on a global commodity -- does not have a wide moat however good its returns look at the top of a cycle. On the energy transition, the threat is manageable rather than terminal on any horizon we underwrite: oil demand is at record highs, and Permian and Bakken barrels are the lowest-cost in America, which makes them the last cut in a shrinking-demand world, not the first.

So the cap never binds, and it does not need to. Value conviction is 2 on the arithmetic alone: a high-quality asset trading about 7% above a fair-value estimate that two independent methods agree on offers no margin of safety, and quality does not substitute for price. Execution conviction is also 2, for the separate reason that the catalyst is spent and the macro tilt is actively hostile. The two scores land in the same place here by coincidence, not by default -- the value case fails on price, the catalyst case fails on timing.

This is a name to admire and revisit, not to own today. The specific level that would make it interesting: the high teens to low twenties -- at or below the adverse case near $17, or meaningfully under the $25.50 fair value -- which a genuine oil flush toward $60 Brent could deliver, most plausibly after the October distribution normalizes and the yield-chasers who bought the July headline discover what they actually bought. Buy the disappointment, not the announcement.
